Introduction

A 'lighting audit' is a count of all the lights in a building, what kind they are, and how often they are on. In this worksheet you will do a small audit of one part of your school - for example one classroom, one corridor, or one toilet area.
Theory

An ENERGY AUDIT is a systematic look at where energy is being used. A LIGHTING AUDIT is the same thing but only for lights. The point of an audit is not to make detailed calculations - that comes later. The point is to FIND OUT what is actually there: how many lights, what kind, when they are on.

Doing an audit is simple but it requires you to be careful and systematic. You walk through one area with a clipboard and write down what you see. You don't just look at the lights - you also pay attention to whether the room is being used or not.

The most important question in a lighting audit is: 'Are these lights on while no-one is using the room?' That is wasted energy. Common places where this happens at school: toilets, corridors during lessons, storage rooms, sports halls between lessons, and offices outside school hours.
Worked example
*Imagine you are auditing your school library.*
**Step 1:** Walk in. Look up at the ceiling. You count: 6 light fixtures, each containing 2 fluorescent tubes. So 12 bulbs in total.
**Step 2:** Ask the librarian (or your teacher): how many hours are the lights on? Answer: from 08:00 to 16:00 = 8 hours per school day.
**Step 3:** Spend 5 minutes observing. You notice: the corner near the window is empty AND has the lights on, even though daylight is bright there.
**Step 4:** Recommendation: switch off the row of lights closest to the window when daylight is enough.
Key terms
Term
Definition
Audit
A systematic check to record what is actually there.
Fixture
The lamp installation in a wall or ceiling. One fixture can hold one or several bulbs.
Wasted lighting
Light that is on while nobody is using the room or while daylight is enough.
Choose your area and count
With your teacher, choose ONE area of the school. Walk through it and count the lights.
Which area did you audit?
How many light fixtures are in this area? (A 'fixture' is one lamp - it can hold one or more bulbs.)
How many individual bulbs in total?
What kind of bulbs are they? (LED tubes, fluorescent tubes, regular bulbs, halogen spots…)
How long are the lights on?
Estimate when the lights in your area are on.
Roughly how many hours per school day are the lights on in this area?
Is this area used in the evening or weekends? If yes, how long?
Are there ANY lights in this area that you noticed are on when nobody is using the room? If yes, how many?
In one or two sentences, write one suggestion to reduce 'wasted' lighting in this area.

After this worksheet, you will be able to give your school three concrete recommendations to reduce lighting energy. You will use measurements and calculations - not opinions - to support those recommendations.
What you should already know
*You should already understand how to perform a basic walk-through audit (see Worksheet 3A), and be confident with energy calculations Energy = Power × time and Cost = Energy × tariff.*

At this level the audit becomes QUANTITATIVE. You don't just observe - you measure and calculate. The output of your audit is a table of numbers: kWh per area, € per area, and (most importantly) the ESTIMATED WASTED hours per area.

WASTED HOURS = total 'lights on' hours minus actual 'occupied' hours. This is your improvement potential. A toilet that is lit for 10 hours per school day but only occupied for 2 hours per day has 8 wasted hours - 80% of its lighting energy is wasted.

RECOMMENDATIONS should be SPECIFIC, MEASURABLE and FINANCIALLY JUSTIFIED. 'Use less light' is not a recommendation. 'Install a motion sensor in toilet block A, saving an estimated 320 kWh and €80 per year' is a recommendation. The facility manager can decide on the basis of that number whether the investment is worth it.

PRIORITISATION: when you have several recommendations, rank them by annual €-saving, not by how easy they are. Easy fixes are nice but they are usually small. The big wins are often spaces with long 'lights on' but short 'occupied' hours.
*Audit of a school corridor.*
**Step 1:** Observe: 8 LED tubes of 24 W each = 192 W total. Lights on 10 hours per school day. School year ≈ 190 days.
**Step 3:** Annual cost at €0.25/kWh: €91.20
**Step 4:** Estimate occupied time: corridor is busy for ~10 minutes between lessons, ~6 times per day = ~1 hour real use
**Step 5:** Wasted hours: 10 - 1 = 9 hours per day (90% of usage)
**Step 6:** Recommendation: motion sensor (€60 installed). Estimated saving: 90% of 364.8 = 328 kWh = €82/year. Payback = 60 / 82 ≈ 0.7 years.
Wasted hours
Hours that lights are on while the space is not in use.
Improvement potential
The maximum energy you could save (= wasted hours × wattage).
Payback period
How long it takes for the savings to pay back the investment.

Schools across Europe are replacing fluorescent and halogen lighting with LED systems. The investment is real (often €30-€80 per fixture for a full LED replacement), and the savings depend strongly on usage. In this worksheet you will design a retrofit business case for your school, using the same tools that an energy consultant would use.
*This worksheet assumes you have completed Worksheet 3B (or are confident with quantitative auditing and basic payback calculations).*

A BUSINESS CASE is a formal document that argues why an investment should (or should not) be made. It includes: (1) the current situation, (2) the proposed change, (3) the financial analysis, (4) the non-financial considerations, (5) a recommendation.

SIMPLE PAYBACK is investment ÷ annual saving. It is intuitive but it ignores the time value of money - €100 saved in 10 years is worth less than €100 saved next year, because money in the future could otherwise have been invested.
NET PRESENT VALUE (NPV) corrects for this. With a discount rate r and annual saving S over n years, the NPV is:
NPV = Σ_{t=1..n} S/(1+r)^t − Investment
If NPV > 0 the project creates value. A typical school discount rate in the EU is 3-5%.

EMBODIED CARBON: every new product carries a carbon debt from its manufacturing. For an LED fixture, this is roughly 20 kg CO₂-equivalent. Replacing a still-working fluorescent fixture means you 'pay' that embodied carbon up front, and only break even on lifecycle emissions after several years of operational savings.

LIGHT QUALITY: lighting is not only about kWh. The EN 12464-1 standard recommends minimum lux levels for different spaces (300 lux for classrooms, 500 lux for sports halls). Under-lit spaces affect concentration and safety. Over-lit spaces waste energy AND can cause discomfort. A good retrofit improves both efficiency and quality.
*Calculate the 10-year NPV of a €5,000 LED retrofit that saves €1,000 per year, with discount rate r=4%.*
**Step 3:** Sum of discounted savings ≈ €8,111
**Step 4:** NPV = 8,111 − 5,000 = €3,111. Project is financially attractive.
**Step 5:** Compare to simple payback: 5000/1000 = 5 years. NPV gives more nuance: even after 10 years the discounted savings are €3,111 above investment.

LED retrofit business case
Assume an LED retrofit costs €50 per fixture (labour included). LED fixtures use about 40% of the wattage of equivalent fluorescent fixtures, and last 50,000 hours.
Compute the new annual kWh after retrofit (assume same 'lights on' hours).

Beyond money
Financial savings are not the only consideration in a retrofit decision.

Use a lux meter (or smartphone app) to measure light levels in 3 different spaces. Compare to the EN 12464-1 recommended values: classrooms 300 lux, corridors 100 lux, sports halls 300-500 lux. Are any spaces under- or over-lit?

Embodied carbon: each new LED fixture has ~20 kg CO₂-equivalent of manufacturing emissions. If you retrofit 200 fixtures, that is 4,000 kg CO₂. How many years of operational savings (vs. fluorescent) does it take to 'pay back' that embodied carbon? Use 0.27 kg CO₂/kWh.
